alex: Quick ask — trying to do short nsys captures (≈5s) to debug a perf regression that shows up in kernel selection + KV cache thrash during mixed batch sizes. What CLI flags do folks use to keep overhead low but still get kernel timelines + NVTX + OSRT events?

maria: For short runs I usually: --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt, limit duration, and use capture-range to clip noise. Example I drop into terminal:```bash
nsys profile -o tmp/short_kv --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-start=nvtx --capture-range-end=nvtx --duration=5s
```
That gets the kernel timeline + NVTX ranges only for the hot window. :thumbsup:

jin: Adding: if you care about sampling-based hotspots, add a sampling interval so you don't flood the trace. I do `--sample=cpu --sample-interval=100us` for wallclock sampling and still get kernel stacks. If you see too much overhead, use `--sample=none` and rely on kernel timestamps only.

alex: Does `--capture-range=nvtx` strictly start/stop around our app NVTX push/pop? We annotate batching/kvcache ops so want to capture only those NVTX ranges. Also any OSRT tips for scheduling jitter?

sam: Yes — capture-range=nvtx uses NVTX markers. Make sure your NVTX push/pop surround the exact hotspot, e.g. `nvtxRangePushA("batch-merge")` before enqueue + `nvtxRangePop()` after. For OSRT: include `--trace=osrt` and set the sampling to a bit coarser (100–200us) to reduce noise. That shows user-space scheduling, host<->device syncs and thread stalls that line up with long kernel tails.

maria: A couple of practical bits: 1) run very short, warm the model once before capture (`curl` or local request) so kernel selection/quantized paths are stable; 2) for environment variance, set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and disable frequency governors; 3) if you want lighter captures, `--trace=cuda,nvtx` without osrt is still helpful for kernel names and NVTX ranges.

jin: When analysing, look for patterns: repeated short memcpy+kernel pairs for KV cache thrash, or a single larger matmul kernel (eg `cublasLtMatmul` / `matmul_fp16`) that takes the tail of the NVTX range. If kernel name changes between runs, that's kernel selection regressing to a slower fallback (quantization mismatch or workspace allocation).

alex: Found one trace — kernel timeline shows `attention_kernel_fp16` vs `attention_kernel_ref` alternating across batches and long gaps aligning with `kv_rebuild` NVTX ranges. Any quick heuristics to decide if it's a batching heuristic bug vs cache eviction?

sam: Heuristic checklist: 1) correlate KV cache size + memcpy ops in trace — if you see repeated large host->device memcpy right before rebuild NVTX, it's eviction. 2) if kernel name switches when batch size crosses a threshold, kernel selection logic probably chose a different algorithm (check workspace or sequence length). 3) enable a couple of extra NVTX ranges inside the runtime where selection happens to capture the decision point.

maria: Also use the timeline's "Instance Count" column for kernels — lots of tiny kernels = batching overhead. If you see a long-running single kernel for the same NVTX range, that's likely a single-model compute path.

perf-bot: Artifact: short capture uploaded -> https://artifacts.internal/redwood/traces/1795554321/short_kv.qdrep 
perf-bot: Quick summary: hotspot around 3.2s — alternating `attention_kernel_fp16` (fast) and `attention_kernel_ref` (3.5x slower). Multiple host->device memcpy bursts at 3.0–3.15s consistent with KV cache refill. Suspect batching heuristic triggers a fallback when batch size mod boundary == 1.

alex: Perfect, thanks. I'll add NVTX around the kernel-selection code path and re-run with `--sample-interval=200us` to get a cleaner OSRT signal. Will post results.
